annotations.title: Meet Riverton: 1,000 residents
annotations.text:
Each bubble is one person. Unlike in real life, we know the truth about every one of them.

So we can watch each kind of bias pull an estimate away from that truth.

Sampling bias: who ends up in the data.
Response bias: what they tell us.

view.title: Who’s in the data — and what they tell you
view.caption: Sampling bias and response bias, one resident at a time

annotations.title: Town average: 122.7 mmHg
annotations.text: To estimate Riverton’s blood pressure, a nurse measures the 89 people sitting in the clinic waiting room one morning (orange).

view.title: Convenience sampling · 1 of 2
view.caption: Sampling whoever is easiest to reach

annotations.title: Waiting room: 135.4 mmHg
annotations.text:
12.7 mmHg too high. People at a clinic are older and sicker than the town as a whole.

Fix: a random sample of the whole town.

view.title: Convenience sampling · 2 of 2
view.caption: The easiest people to reach are not typical

annotations.title: Town average: 6.8 / 10
annotations.text: The clinic posts an online poll: “Rate our new opening hours.” 92 people choose to answer (orange).

view.title: Voluntary response · 1 of 2
view.caption: People choose themselves to be in the sample

annotations.title: Poll average: 4.7 / 10
annotations.text:
The poll says the hours are unpopular. The angry (and a few delighted) speak up; the content majority stays quiet.

Fix: pick respondents at random — don’t let them pick themselves.

view.title: Voluntary response · 2 of 2
view.caption: Strong feelings — especially negative ones — get people to respond

annotations.title: Town average: 166 min a week
annotations.text: A health survey is run online. The 169 residents without internet (grey) — 54% of them over 65 — can never be sampled.

view.title: Under-coverage · 1 of 2
view.caption: Part of the population has no chance of being sampled

annotations.title: Online average: 182 min a week
annotations.text:
Even a perfectly random online sample overstates exercise: the people it can’t reach are older and less active.

Fix: a sampling frame that covers everyone (mail, phone, in person).

view.title: Under-coverage · 2 of 2
view.caption: The sampling frame (internet users) is not the population

annotations.title: Random 300: 4.6 drinks a week
annotations.text:
300 residents chosen at random are mailed an alcohol survey. That sample is fair (the town average is 4.8).

But only the orange ones send it back.

view.title: Non-response bias · 1 of 2
view.caption: A random sample is chosen — but not everyone in it answers

annotations.title: Returned: 2.8 drinks a week
annotations.text:
Only 171 of 300 reply, and heavy drinkers are the least likely to. A random start doesn’t help if the replies aren’t random.

Fix: follow up non-responders; keep surveys short.

view.title: Non-response bias · 2 of 2
view.caption: The people who don’t answer differ from those who do

annotations.title: True BP: 121.5 vs 123.9
annotations.text: Half the town is measured with a blood-pressure cuff that is out of calibration (orange). Their true pressures are the same as everyone else’s.

view.title: Measurement bias · 1 of 2
view.caption: The measuring instrument itself is wrong

annotations.title: Measured: 131.4 vs 124
annotations.text:
The faulty cuff adds about 10 mmHg to every reading. A bigger sample won’t help — it just measures the wrong value more precisely.

Fix: calibrate and check instruments against a standard.

view.title: Measurement bias · 2 of 2
view.caption: Every reading is pushed the same way

annotations.title: Actual: 166 min a week
annotations.text: Exercise measured by a wrist tracker. Now we simply ask: “How many minutes did you exercise last week?”

view.title: Social desirability bias · 1 of 2
view.caption: People give the answer that makes them look good

annotations.title: Reported: 212 min a week
annotations.text:
Everyone drifts right, and the least active (orange) exaggerate the most.

Fix: anonymous questions, neutral wording, objective measures.

view.title: Social desirability bias · 2 of 2
view.caption: Good behaviour is over-reported; bad behaviour is under-reported

annotations.title: Diary: 2.5 vs 2.1 meals
annotations.text: Fast-food meals a week ten years ago, from old food diaries. The 70 heart patients (orange) really did eat a little more.

view.title: Recall bias · 1 of 2
view.caption: Some groups remember the past better than others

annotations.title: Recalled: 4 vs 1.4 meals
annotations.text:
Asked to remember instead, patients over-recall and everyone else under-recalls. A small real difference now looks huge.

Fix: use records made at the time.

view.title: Recall bias · 2 of 2
view.caption: Patients search their memory for a cause; healthy people forget

annotations.title: True: 4.7 vs 4.7
annotations.text: 240 patients get either a new drug (orange) or a placebo. The drug does nothing: both groups improve the same.

view.title: Observer bias · 1 of 2
view.caption: What researchers expect to see shapes what they record

annotations.title: Doctor’s rating: 6 vs 4.4
annotations.text:
Rating patients they know got the drug, the doctor sees an effect that isn’t there.

Fix: blinding — neither patient nor assessor knows who got what.

view.title: Observer bias · 2 of 2
view.caption: The doctor knows who got the drug — and expects it to work

annotations.title: Usual: 7,307 steps a day
annotations.text: Everyone’s normal daily steps, from their phones. Then the clinic announces a “step study” and hands out trackers for a week…

view.title: The Hawthorne effect · 1 of 2
view.caption: People change their behaviour when they know they’re being studied

annotations.title: Study week: 8,717 steps a day
annotations.text:
Nobody lied: they really walked 1,410 more steps a day — because they were being watched.

Fix: a control group observed the same way; longer, unobtrusive measurement.

view.title: The Hawthorne effect · 2 of 2
view.caption: Being watched is itself a treatment

annotations.title: True: 4.8 vs 4.8 drinks
annotations.text: Each resident is interviewed by A or B at random, so the two groups drink about the same.

view.title: Interviewer bias · 1 of 2
view.caption: Who asks the question — and how — changes the answer

annotations.title: Reported: 2.6 vs 4.5 drinks
annotations.text:
Same kind of people, different interviewer, different data.

Fix: trained interviewers with a script; self-completed answers for sensitive questions.

view.title: Interviewer bias · 2 of 2
view.caption: Interviewer A frowns at the answers; interviewer B stays neutral

annotations.title: Sampling bias — who’s in the data
annotations.text:
• Convenience → random sampling
• Voluntary response → choose people at random
• Under-coverage → a frame that includes everyone
• Non-response → follow up; keep it short

annotations.title: Response bias — what they tell you
annotations.text:
• Measurement → calibrate instruments
• Social desirability → anonymous, neutral questions
• Recall → records made at the time
• Observer → blinding
• Hawthorne → an observed control group
• Interviewer → training, scripts, self-completion

view.title: Guarding against bias
view.caption: A bigger sample doesn’t fix bias — a better design does
